s1.title: cmpctblock has no anti-DoS work threshold, and the anti-replay gate only fires for headers already in the index — every replay rebuilds the whole-mempool short-ID map
s1.our_ref: src/networking/protocol.lisp:3515 (compact-block-header-verdict 3467-3573); build-shortid-map src/networking/protocol.lisp:3266; mempool maphash src/mempool/mempool.lisp:1861; rate-limit fallthrough src/networking/peer.lisp:1828-1841
evidence:
CONFIRM: CORE (read, verbatim): refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:4578-4582 is `else if (prev_block->nChainWork + GetBlockProof(cmpctblock.header) < GetAntiDoSWorkThreshold()) { LogDebug(BCLog::NET, "Ignoring low-work compact block from peer %d\n", ...); return; }`, placed BEFORE ProcessNewBlockHeaders (:4590). PartiallyDownloadedBlock::InitData (:4674) is reached only past that plus `pindex->nChainWork <= Tip()->nChainWork || pindex->nTx != 0` (:4641), `!already_in_flight && !CanDirectFetch()` (:4655), `pindex->nHeight <= Height()+2` (:4661), AND a fifth gate the finder did not mention: the "Peer sent us compact block we were already syncing!" early return (:4670).

OURS (read): compact-block-header-verdict spans src/networking/protocol.lisp:3467-3572 and contains NO work threshold. `grep -rn "anti-dos\|work-threshold" src/` returns exactly two hits, both in src/networking/headers-sync.lisp (defun at :377, sole use in maybe-start-presync at :414) — the check has not moved, it is absent from this path. The only work comparison is inside the `(and known ...)` arm at :3515-3521. The docstring states the function is "Pure reads of the block index"; it never inserts the header, and handle-cmpctblock (:3574-3715) never inserts it either, so KNOWN stays NIL across replays and the :already-have anti-replay arm can never fire for an unseen header. Dispatch at :312-315 gates only on `(when mempool ...)` — no IBD, sendcmpct, or work gate. build-shortid-map (:3266) calls bl.mp:mempool-for-each, which is a bare `(maphash fn (mempool-entries mempool))` at src/mempool/mempool.lisp:1858-1861; reconstruct-compact-block calls it unconditionally after only the (zerop tx-count)/(> tx-count 100000) guard. check-peer-rate-limit (src/networking/peer.lisp:1825-1841) has no "cmpctblock" arm and falls through to `t`.

EXECUTED (scripts/dev.sh eval, warm image). Regtest chain-state with genesis indexed, bl::*minimum-chain-work-override* = 2^240 to model a real network's minimum chain work, one PoW-valid header ground off genesis:
  anti-dos-work-threshold  = 1766847064778384329583297500742918515827483896875618958121606201292619776
  header claimed chainwork = 3
  Core would IGNORE it?    = T
  OUR verdict pass 1       = ACCEPT / NIL / T
  header indexed after?    = NIL
  OUR verdict pass 2       = ACCEPT / NIL / T
  rate-limit for cmpctblock= T
So: Core ignores it, we return :ACCEPT, the header is still not in the index afterwards, and the identical second call returns :ACCEPT again — the replay loop is real, and cmpctblock is unrate-limited.

EXECUTED (cost of the pass that :ACCEPT unlocks). 50,000-entry mempool, three consecutive build-shortid-map passes:
  pass 0: 0.059 s, 80.1 MB consed   (first pass also computes+caches wtxids)
  pass 1: 0.015 s, 16.0 MB consed
  pass 2: 0.015 s, 16.0 MB consed
i.e. a ~100-byte attacker message buys ~15 ms CPU and 16 MB of garbage on the message-processing thread, repeatable without limit and without misbehaviour scoring.

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED: validate-block-header (src/validation/block.lisp:655-719) checks PoW, +max-future-block-time+, MTP, BIP94, the softfork version floor and difficulty bits only — no work floor, no checkpoint, so the (t ...) arm really does reach :ACCEPT on header validity alone. +max-messages-per-peer-per-cycle+ (32, src/networking/ibd.lisp:33) is a per-pump-cycle fairness bound, not a rate limit. testnet-min-difficulty-allowed-p exists (src/validation/block.lisp:437-443), so on testnet3/testnet4 the one-time header really is free. The tree's own comment at protocol.lisp:3410-3414 already names this exact DoS shape ("one connection can replay an invalid-PoW cmpctblock without limit, each replay costing a full BUILD-SHORTID-MAP SipHash pass") and closed only the invalid-PoW variant by punishing; the valid-PoW low-work variant — precisely what Core's GetAntiDoSWorkThreshold exists for — is left open.

ONE CORRECTION IN THE FINDER'S FAVOUR: handle-cmpctblock keeps peer-pending-compact-block when the replayed hash MATCHES (it clears only on a different hash, :3636-3641), so a replay while our getblocktxn is outstanding re-runs the full map build and emits another getblocktxn — Core returns early there. The finding is if anything understated.

CONFIRM: EXECUTED (warm image, scripts/dev.sh eval). Built a 200-entry regtest block index, set the tip, and called the real function with a genuinely PoW-valid header forked at height 5 (regtest powLimit bits, timestamp=now, so check-proof-of-work, MTP, version floor and validate-difficulty all pass honestly):
  (:VERDICT :ACCEPT :REASON NIL :CREDIT NIL :ATTACKER-CHAIN-WORK 13 :TIP-WORK 401 :ANTI-DOS-THRESHOLD 113 :HEADER-IN-INDEX NIL)
bl.net::compact-block-header-verdict returns :ACCEPT for a header below BOTH Core gates: the anti-DoS floor (113, from our own bl.net::anti-dos-work-threshold) and the tip work (401). Core would have returned at net_processing.cpp:4578-4582 ("Ignoring low-work compact block") and again at :4645 (nChainWork <= tip), both BEFORE InitData at :4679. GetAntiDoSWorkThreshold confirmed at net_processing.cpp:2635.

EXECUTED: build-shortid-map over a 50,000-entry mempool -> (:SECONDS-PER-PASS 0.013 :BYTES-PER-PASS 6413821). This REFUTES the finder's magnitude (claimed 0.2-0.3 s and ~50 MB per second; actual ~13 ms / 6.4 MB per replay -- transaction-wtxid is cached at src/serialization/types.lisp:435).

EXECUTED: (check-peer-rate-limit peer "cmpctblock") returned T for 10,000 consecutive calls. Source-decisive anyway: src/networking/peer.lisp:1825-1841 has no "cmpctblock" clause, so bucket is NIL and the function returns T.

READ, traced personally:
- src/networking/headers-sync.lisp:377 anti-dos-work-threshold exists; its ONLY caller is :414 (maybe-start-presync). Nothing in the cmpctblock path.
- src/networking/protocol.lisp:3515 the work comparison is inside the (and known ...) arm only. The (t ...) arm at :3562-3571 DOES compute (calculate-chain-work bits prev-work) > tip-work but uses it solely for credits-announcement, never as a gate -- the right number is computed and discarded. (Minor imprecision in the finder's wording; it strengthens rather than weakens the finding.)
- src/validation/block.lisp:655 validate-block-header has no minimum-work / anti-DoS check; PoW, 2h future, MTP, BIP94, version floor, difficulty bits only.
- src/networking/protocol.lisp:312 dispatch is unconditional -- no sendcmpct negotiation gate, no IBD gate, no permission gate; only peer-state :ready (free handshake). ibd.lisp:1628 dispatch-ibd-message falls straight through to handle-message for cmpctblock.
- src/networking/protocol.lisp:3636-3642 keeps the pending reconstruction when the hash matches and reconstructs again anyway -- no dedup. On missing-indexes we send getblocktxn and the header is never inserted into the index, so the identical message replays forever. record-misbehavior on this path fires only for :malformed and blocktxn mismatch.
- src/networking/protocol.lisp:3289 reconstruct-compact-block does only the tx-count sanity check before build-shortid-map; src/mempool/mempool.lisp:1861 is a bare maphash, no lock.
- Single-threaded: grep make-thread over src/networking/ returns only torcontrol.lisp:715. ibd.lisp:1849 pump-peer-messages is (dolist (peer peers) (drain-and-reap-peer ...)) on the sync thread.

CORRECTED IMPACT (still S1): the drain caps a peer at +max-messages-per-peer-per-cycle+ 32 and +max-recv-bytes-per-peer-per-cycle+ 65536 (ibd.lisp:33, :1784, :1805), so one connection buys ~32 x 13 ms = 0.42 s of the node's ONLY network thread per pump cycle for ~4 KB/s of traffic, and peers are drained sequentially, so a handful of connections wedge the pump (pings unanswered, headers/blocks unprocessed). The map is built outside the node lock, so validation/RPC locking is not blocked -- the loss is network-thread liveness.

COST TO ATTACKER IS LOWER THAN CLAIMED, not higher: no testnet min-difficulty argument is needed. Any mainnet header forked at an early height carries bits=0x1d00ffff (difficulty 1, ~2^32 hashes, minutes of CPU, reusable forever against every node), and any publicly archived stale/orphan header at a low height that is not in our index costs nothing at all.

Verdict: unauthenticated, no rate limit, no misbehaviour score, unbounded replay, on the single network thread = remote DoS any peer can trigger. S1 stands; only the per-second CPU/memory figures need correcting.

s1.title: Transaction deserializer accepts the BIP144 extended encoding with all-empty witness stacks; Core throws 'Superfluous witness record'
s1.our_ref: src/serialization/types.lisp:209-232 (br-read-transaction), same gap at types.lisp:266-289 (read-transaction); transaction-has-witness-p types.lisp:169-173
evidence:
CONFIRM: MECHANISM CONFIRMED — both citations are verbatim accurate and no guard exists elsewhere.

CORE: refs/bitcoin/src/primitives/transaction.h:222-231 reads exactly as filed — `if ((flags & 1) && fAllowWitness) { flags ^= 1; for (i...) s >> tx.vin[i].scriptWitness.stack; if (!tx.HasWitness()) throw std::ios_base::failure("Superfluous witness record"); }`. HasWitness() at transaction.h:392-398 loops vin and returns true only on a non-null scriptWitness.

OURS: src/serialization/types.lisp:214-232 (br-read-transaction) — `(unless (= flag 1) (serialization-error "Invalid witness flag byte: ~D" flag))` is the ONLY flag check; it then reads `(%read-n-vector input-count (br-read-witness-stack br))` and calls make-transaction with `:witness witness`. No emptiness test. Identical gap at types.lisp:270-289 (read-transaction). transaction-has-witness-p at types.lisp:169-173 is `(and (transaction-witness tx) (some (lambda (stack) (and stack (not (null stack)))) ...))`, which is NIL for the #(NIL) vector that br-read-witness-stack produces from a zero-item stack — so the tx is treated as legacy exactly as the finder says.

NOT HANDLED ELSEWHERE (grepped, not assumed): `grep -rni superfluous src/` returns only SERIALIZE-side comments (types.lisp:422 in transaction-wire-bytes, rpc/mining.lisp:52) and test prose — nothing rejects it on read. parse-tx-payload (src/serialization/messages.lisp:441-458) enforces only "payload consumed whole" (`(unless (= (br-pos stream) (length payload)) ...)`), which this encoding satisfies. br-read-bitcoin-block (types.lisp:563-569) adds no check. No caller of transaction-has-witness-p in src/validation/ (block.lisp:1088,1141,1170; transaction.lisp:1175,1303) rejects the shape. tests/fuzz-property-tests.lisp:160 only asserts callers guard the ENCODER; its mutants are grown from a legacy base tx and would need two coordinated byte edits to reach marker+flag, so the roundtrip property never exercises this.

SEVERITY OVERSTATED — the "chain the network will not follow" impact does not hold. Nothing re-emits the received bytes: store-block writes `(bl.ser:serialize-witness-block block)` (src/storage/blocks.lisp:387) and make-block-message does the same (src/serialization/messages.lisp:430-438); serialize-witness-block (types.lisp:578-586) selects legacy per-tx via transaction-has-witness-p. Because txid and merkle root come from the legacy serialization, the header hash is identical under both encodings — so we serve Core THE SAME BLOCK in canonical form and Core accepts it. Any divergence is transient and we are the healing node, not a stranded one. Tx relay normalizes the same way through transaction-wire-bytes (types.lisp:416-424). GA9 already recorded this gap as S3 (docs/gap-analysis-9.md:366-368); its stated reason ("a non-canonical encoding enters our block store") is itself too strong, since the store normalizes. Real residual gap: an accept-more divergence at the parse layer (we deserialize bytes Core declares undeserializable, so sendrawtransaction/tx/block messages Core rejects as malformed are accepted by us) — worth the two-line fix, not S1.

EXECUTION UNAVAILABLE: scripts/dev.sh start failed with "failed to connect to the docker API at unix:///Users/sen/.docker/run/docker.sock ... no such file or directory"; host SBCL is forbidden by policy, so the constructed payload 02000000000101c1..c1 0000000000 ffffffff 01 e803000000000000 16 0014751e76e8199196d454941c45d1b3a323f1433bd6 00 00000000 could not be fed to parse-tx-payload. Verdict is read-traced end to end.

CONFIRM: MECHANISM CONFIRMED BY EXECUTION (I did not take the finder's word for it).

Core, read verbatim at refs/bitcoin/src/primitives/transaction.h:222-231: after `if ((flags & 1) && fAllowWitness)` it reads a stack per vin, then `if (!tx.HasWitness()) throw std::ios_base::failure("Superfluous witness record")`. Ours, src/serialization/types.lisp:216-232, checks only `(= flag 1)` and returns; same gap in the stream reader at 274-289. No emptiness check anywhere.

EXECUTED #1 (tx level, warm image). Built the hostile encoding from a real tx via SERIALIZE-WITNESS-TRANSACTION:
  02000000 0001 01<vin> 01<vout> 00 00000000  (the exact "flags=1, all stacks empty" shape Core throws on)
  => (:PARSED T :HAS-WITNESS NIL :WITNESS-SLOT #(NIL) :TXID-SAME T :WTXID-EQ-TXID T :WEIGHT 328
      :RENORMALIZED "0200000001c1e1...bd600000000")
PARSE-TX-PAYLOAD accepts it (its only strictness check, messages.lisp:441-458, is trailing bytes), TRANSACTION-HAS-WITNESS-P is NIL, and TRANSACTION-WIRE-BYTES re-emits the legacy bytes.

EXECUTED #2 (block level). Block = 80-byte header | count 2 | canonical tx | hostile tx:
  (:BAD-BYTES-LEN 248 :GOOD-BYTES-LEN 245 :BAD-BLOCK-PARSED T :BAD-TX-COUNT 2
   :SAME-HEADER-HASH T :SAME-MERKLE-ROOT T :BAD-RESERIALIZES-TO-GOOD T)
PARSE-BLOCK-PAYLOAD (messages.lisp:519-525 -> br-read-bitcoin-block, types.lisp:563-569) accepts it with no post-parse check, and SERIALIZE-WITNESS-BLOCK of the parsed result is byte-identical to the canonical 245-byte block.

WHY THE S1 IMPACT DOES NOT FOLLOW (Lens B). That last executed line is the refutation of the consequence: after parsing, our in-memory block is indistinguishable from the canonical one, and every outbound path re-serializes from the struct, never from the received bytes —
  - store-block writes (bl.ser:serialize-witness-block block), src/storage/blocks.lisp:387 with the comment at 380-386; the hostile bytes never reach disk;
  - make-block-message re-serializes from the struct (messages.lisp:431-439); make-tx-message uses TRANSACTION-WIRE-BYTES (messages.lisp:421-429), guarded by TRANSACTION-HAS-WITNESS-P (types.lisp:416-425);
  - relay-block (protocol.lisp:3053-3071) announces headers/inv only, and the body we then serve is the canonical encoding.
So a relaying bitcoin-lisp node does not "follow a chain the network will not" — it launders the block into the encoding Core accepts and the network converges on the SAME hash. The attacker gains nothing over publishing the canonical form of the very same block: same header, same merkle root, same PoW (executed: SAME-HEADER-HASH T / SAME-MERKLE-ROOT T). The mempool half of the impact is inert for the same reason: the parsed tx is the canonical legacy tx (same txid, wtxid, weight) and we forward it normalized.

REACHABILITY, precisely. The PARSE divergence is ungated — handle-block (protocol.lisp:1069) and dispatch-ibd-message (ibd.lisp:1635) parse any peer's payload with no permission, rate or height gate — but a parse divergence with an identical parse result is not a state divergence. The ACCEPTANCE divergence needs a valid PoW block. The worst residual case is a node with relay disabled (mainnet default, gate at protocol.lisp:3061 `(unless (relay-enabled-p) ...)`): it accepts B, does not announce it, and sits one block ahead until the network out-works it and we reorg. That is strictly weaker than plain block withholding, which needs no bug at all: any miner able to mine B can create exactly that divergence by sending a canonical B only to the target. The bug adds no new capability, no cost reduction, no fund-loss path, no crash and no DoS.

VERDICT: real, correctly read, worth fixing (Core-parity in the "we are more permissive" direction, where splits come from, and only an incidental normalization is standing between it and a real split — any future path that stores or forwards raw received block bytes turns it into one). But S2, not S1.

SEPARATE LEAD FOUND WHILE VERIFYING (opposite direction, not this finding): messages.lisp:569 (cmpctblock prefilled-txs :write) and message-macro.lisp:122 (:witness-transaction field) call SERIALIZE-WITNESS-TRANSACTION UNCONDITIONALLY, so for a witnessless tx we would EMIT the superfluous encoding that Core throws on. The claim in tests/fuzz-property-tests.lisp:160 that "every caller in the tree guards it with TRANSACTION-HAS-WITNESS-P" is false of those two sites. I did not chase its reachability (a segwit coinbase always has the reserved-value witness, so the common case is safe).

s1.title: Block bodies are written to disk with no CheckBlock at all on the two IBD persist paths, and a present-but-invalid body is never re-requested
s1.our_ref: src/networking/ibd.lisp:3858-3862 (out-of-order persist), src/networking/ibd.lisp:3644-3649 (competing-fork persist), src/validation/block.lisp:4102-4110 (activate-block case 3); download walk skip ibd.lisp:1130; queue-missing-fork-blocks ibd.lisp:3382; get-block prune-on-deserialize-failure storage/blocks.lisp:427-440
evidence:
CONFIRM: CORE (read, confirmed): refs/bitcoin/src/validation.cpp:4382-4383 `if (!CheckBlock(block,...) || !ContextualCheckBlock(block,..., pindex->pprev))` -> InvalidBlockFound + return false, placed after the anti-DoS gate (4348-4378) and BEFORE `m_blockman.WriteBlock(block, pindex->nHeight)` at 4405. ProcessNewBlock also CheckBlocks at 4448 before AcceptBlock. Finder's Core claim is exact.

OURS (read, confirmed): src/networking/ibd.lisp:3293 `%out-of-order-block-acceptable-p` docstring literally cites "validation.cpp:4367-4378" — the anti-DoS gate only, the lines just above the CheckBlock it omits. Persist sites: ibd.lisp ~3861-3866 (out-of-order: `(bl.store:note-block-position ... (bl.store:store-block block-store block :height height))` guarded only by `block-witness-stripped-p` + that gate); ibd.lisp ~3645-3651 (competing fork h<=tip: store-block guarded only by `block-witness-stripped-p`, no gate at all); src/validation/block.lisp:4094-4113 activate-block case 3 (same); plus block.lisp:3937-3951 historical-chainstate target filter (same). bl.store:store-block (src/storage/blocks.lisp:366) validates nothing.

EXECUTED 1 (scripts/dev.sh eval, warm image): built a fixture chain to tip h=2, indexed a valid header for h5, then fed process-received-block a FORGED block = that valid header + a different block's coinbase list, :requested t. Output:
(:WITNESS-STRIPPED-P NIL :MERKLE-MATCHES NIL :CHECK-BLOCK-VERDICT (NIL :BAD-MERKLE-ROOT) :PROCESS-RETURNED NIL :BLOCK-EXISTS-P T :READ-BACK-P T)
Same probe on the competing-fork arm (entry height 1, prev=genesis, tip=2) returned byte-identical output. So bl.val::%check-block itself says :BAD-MERKLE-ROOT on the very object that block-exists-p reports as persisted — the check exists and is simply not on these two paths.

EXECUTED 2 (never re-requested): synthetic peer chain h3..h6 above tip, peer :ready with NODE_NETWORK|NODE_WITNESS. `find-blocks-to-download-for-peer peer cs store 10` returned (d003 d004 d005 d006). After a single `bl.store:store-block` under h4's hash and resetting peer-last-common-block-hash to NIL, the same call returned (d003 d005 d006) with :H4-ON-DISK T. The block-exists-p arm at ibd.lisp:1129-1131 also advances the peer cursor past it.

NOT HANDLED ELSEWHERE (checked): src/networking/protocol.lisp:944-1030 accept-downloaded-block DOES call bl.val:validate-block (:context-free-only t for side branches), but src/networking/ibd.lisp:1632-1710 dispatch-ibd-message handles command "block" itself and calls process-received-block, never falling through to handle-message — so the validated path is not the IBD path. Recovery paths all dead: request-blocks-from-peers (ibd.lisp:1356-1508) issues getdata only from find-blocks-to-download-for-peer / find-historical-blocks-to-download, never from pending-blocks, so handle-validation-failure's re-add (ibd.lisp:531-534, budget 3 then silent) is a dead letter — a fact queue-missing-fork-blocks' own docstring (ibd.lisp:445-449) states. get-block (src/storage/blocks.lisp:427-455) prunes only on a deserialize raise; a wrong-merkle body deserializes fine (:READ-BACK-P T above). drain-block-queue (ibd.lisp:3928-4005) re-loads it from disk via %next-disk-block-for-drain every cycle, so the tip can never pass that height.

CITATION SLIP (substance intact): queue-missing-fork-blocks is at ibd.lisp:439, not 3382 (3382 is inside %park-unlinked-reorg-candidate). Its behaviour matches the finding — it only queues hashes perform-reorg reported ABSENT from the store.

Note on scope: a bad body cannot enter the chain (tip+1 goes through activate-block case 1 -> validate-block, which stores only inside connect-block), so this is not a consensus split. It is a remote unauthenticated permanent sync wedge from any peer we requested a block from, plus we would serve the invalid body on getdata. S1 stands.

CONFIRM: SURVIVES. Traced all three persist sites and settled two legs by execution.

REACHABILITY (no gate stops it): dispatch-ibd-message (src/networking/ibd.lisp:1628) parses a "block" message and calls process-received-block with zero body checks. `requested` = (or in-flight pending) at ibd.lisp:1684-1686, and pending is filled with EVERY newly-synced header (ibd.lisp:929-934), so %out-of-order-block-acceptable-p (ibd.lisp:3293-3308) short-circuits on `requested` for every block we still want — Core's anti-DoS gate is a no-op during IBD. run-ibd gets (node-peers node) (src/node/sync.lisp:59), which includes INBOUND peers (src/node/eviction.lisp:23), so any connected peer, not just the one we asked, can push the body. No rate limit, no permission gate, no work gate.

EXECUTED 1 (scripts/dev.sh eval, warm image) — poisoned block = b3's header + b2's tx list (same block hash, merkle mismatch):
  (:ROOTS-DIFFER T :MERKLE-VERDICT (NIL :BAD-MERKLE-ROOT NIL) :PERSISTED-OUT-OF-ORDER T :TIP-NOW 2 :ACTIVATE-RESULT (NIL :BAD-VERSION) :STILL-ON-DISK-AFTER-FAILURE T :DISK-COPY-IS-POISON T)
So the merkle-mismatched body IS written to disk by the out-of-order arm, and after the later connect attempt fails it is still on disk and still the poisoned bytes.

EXECUTED 2 — with a body on disk for height 2 only, find-blocks-to-download-for-peer returns (1 3 4): height 2 is skipped purely on block-exists-p (ibd.lisp:1130-1146). request-blocks-from-peers (ibd.lisp:1469) has no other source, so pending is a dead letter for requests — queue-missing-fork-blocks' own docstring says so (ibd.lisp:948-960; the finder's "3382" cite is wrong, that line is %parked-candidate-blocked-p).

NO RECOVERY: forget-block-body fires only for witness-STRIPPED bodies inside perform-reorg (src/validation/block.lisp:3503-3512). :bad-merkle-root is deliberately excluded from *deterministic-invalid-block-errors* so nothing is poisoned/marked, and handle-validation-failure (ibd.lisp:503-538) only re-adds to the dead-letter pending. getblockfrompeer refuses with "Block already downloaded" when block-exists-p is true (src/rpc/blockchain.lisp:2610), so even the manual operator lever is blocked. check-stuck-tip eventually halts IBD.

PERSIST SITES VERIFIED verbatim: ibd.lisp:3858-3862 (out-of-order store-block), ibd.lisp:3644-3649 (competing-fork store-block), block.lisp:4102-4110 (activate-block case 3). Only guard on all three is block-witness-stripped-p (block.lisp:1188-1195), which inspects the coinbase witness only. Core's AcceptBlock runs CheckBlock+ContextualCheckBlock at refs/bitcoin/src/validation.cpp:4382-4389 immediately before WriteBlock at :4400.

WHERE THE FINDER OVERREACHES (does not change severity): this is NOT a consensus split. perform-reorg runs a full validate-block per connected fork block including merkle, with :skip-header t (block.lisp:3223-3245), and the tip+1 arm validates too, so an invalid body is never applied to the UTXO set. Note also block.lisp:2966-2971 asserts fork blocks "ALREADY PASSED" CheckBlock at store time — true for protocol.lisp accept-downloaded-block (:1016-1029), FALSE for all three IBD sites, an in-tree confirmation of the gap.

S1 stands on the DoS limb alone: unauthenticated, single message from any connected peer, permanent sync wedge at an attacker-chosen height, recoverable only by deleting the block file.

s1.title: BIP143/BIP341 sighash writes nVersion through buf-set-u32-le, which is declared (unsigned-byte 32) while transaction-version is (signed-byte 32)
s1.our_ref: src/coalton/interop.lisp:1859 (bip143), src/coalton/interop.lisp:3195-3197 (bip341); slot type src/serialization/types.lisp:152 filled by br-read-i32-le at types.lisp:214; macro declaration src/util/bytes.lisp:41-51 instantiated at :54; contrast bb-write-u32-le masking at src/util/bytes.lisp:126-133
evidence:
CONFIRM: CONFIRMED by execution; I could not refute it on any lens.

CORE (read): refs/bitcoin/src/script/interpreter.cpp:1646 is `ss << txTo.version;` under the `// Version` comment in the BIP143 branch of SignatureHash; :1520 is `ss << tx_to.version;` under `// Transaction level data` in SignatureHashSchnorr. Both as the finder described.

ONE FINDER ERROR, IMMATERIAL: at d3056bc CTransaction::version is `const uint32_t` (refs/bitcoin/src/primitives/transaction.h:293; CMutableTransaction `uint32_t` at :361), NOT int32_t as the finding states. This does not weaken the claim -- it strengthens it: Core deliberately made the full 32-bit range well-defined, and there is no consensus rule on version (only policy). ## 4. What this method structurally cannot see

Reading two trees side by side compares **definitions**. It cannot compare **executions**. Nine defect classes are therefore invisible by construction, not by budget:

**1. Concurrency: races, lock ordering, shared mutable state.** 97 lock sites across 15 files, 12 `make-thread` sites across 8 files. Core encodes this contract in the *type system* — `GUARDED_BY`, `EXCLUSIVE_LOCKS_REQUIRED`, `AssertLockHeld` — so a static reader of C++ sees the invariant on the line. A static reader of our Lisp sees nothing, and **both files that document our discipline (`src/node/state.lisp`, `src/rpc/accessors.lisp`) were never opened.** GA10 stumbled into exactly one instance (`*last-checksig-error*` / `*last-checkmultisig-error*` are process globals clobbered by parallel script workers) and it is unverified. *Most exposed:* the recursive `node-lock` under concurrent RPC handler threads + sync thread + inbound listener + parallel script-check pool + wallet hooks; `src/mempool/mempool.lisp`; addrman; per-peer send/receive queues; `src/util/ratelimit.lisp`'s unlocked-by-assumption buckets. *Tool:* a lock-order assertion pass plus a concurrency stress test (N RPC threads against a live sync), not another reader.

**2. Liveness: blocking I/O, deadlock, starvation, backpressure.** Our worst production bugs are all in this class and *none* was ever found by a gap analysis: `receive-bytes` blocking forever in `read-sequence` (a 24-byte header + silence froze the whole node — remote unauth DoS); `SEND-BYTES NEVER BLOCKS` (unbounded send-queue growth, root cause of a 1-in-3 cold-battery flake); the `select()` fd>1023 type-error that killed every mainnet peer. Each one reads perfectly on the page. GA10's unverified "a backed-up send buffer makes us DROP outbound messages" is the same family and needs a run to settle. *Tool:* an adversarial peer harness (slow-loris, half-open, dead-air, flood) and a long soak.

**3. Algorithmic complexity and resource growth.** Reading tells you what Core does, never how long ours takes. History: block *deserialization* was the IBD bottleneck (not signature verification, which is where everyone looked); an 83MB mempool.dat turned restart into a 45-minute silent outage; header-index write amplification; 25 functional-test "timeouts" that were one shared *slowness*, not a hang. *Most exposed:* `src/mempool/txgraph.lisp` + `cluster-linearize.lisp` (unread, and linearization is where superlinear blowups live), `src/storage/chain.lisp`, `src/networking/ibd.lisp`. *Tool:* profiling + a bounded-time assertion in the cold battery.

**4. Round-trip and boundary-value divergence.** Core ships **138 fuzz harnesses**; we have `tests/fuzz-property-tests.lisp` (283 lines, 12 properties, explicitly *not* libFuzzer — no coverage guidance, no sanitizer, no corpus minimization). Every finding of this shape GA10 produced by *reading* is unverified: the BIP144 all-empty-witness acceptance, the lax-DER divergence "in both directions," the unbounded `base58-decode`, the coinbase wtxid reported as 32 zero bytes. *Most exposed:* `src/serialization/*` (esp. the never-read `message-macro.lisp` that generates them all), `src/util/bytes.lisp`, `src/crypto/address.lisp`, `src/serialization/psbt.lisp`, `src/rpc/descriptors.lisp`, `src/storage/blockfilter.lisp` (GCS). *Tool:* a differential harness — same bytes into ours and into Core's `bitcoin-tx`/`bitcoin-util`/a fuzz target, compare verdicts. This is the highest-leverage thing GA11 could build.

**5. The "correct code, no caller / wrong caller" class.** Our history names it **at least fourteen times** ("14th no-caller bug", "12th 'correct code, wrong callers'"; `build-tx-index` had no caller; txindex maintained only by startup catch-up; 5 of 6 activation sites never passed `:tx-index`; reorg only triggered by an arriving block; ms-satisfy never wired into the signer). Two-tree reading compares definitions; it does not compare *who calls them, how often, and with what arguments*. GA10 caught one only by accident (`HANDLE-MESSAGE`'s `block`/`headers` arms are dead because `DISPATCH-IBD-MESSAGE` intercepts first). *Tool:* a mechanical call-graph/reachability diff, or coverage instrumentation over the cold battery — anything reached zero times by 34k checks is a candidate.

**6. State-machine divergence that needs N transitions.** Both of this round's S1s are of this shape: the FRESH/DIRTY flag needs a `gettxoutsetinfo` **then** a spend **then** a re-lookup; the flat-file scan needs a prune **then** a restart. Reading can only *hypothesize* these; ten minutes of a real pruned node would settle both. Same family: the `*cached-is-ibd*` one-way latch, the prune watermark that stops reclaiming space, addrman table saturation past `ADDRMAN_RETRIES`, deep-reorg candidate parking. *Most exposed:* pruning, restart/crash recovery, reorg, addrman.

**7. Timing, cadence, and scheduling.** Poisson addr/tx broadcast timers, feeler cadence, ping timeouts, headers-sync timeouts, fee-estimator decay, the eviction rotation. Reading gives the constant; only a run gives the emergent behaviour. GA10's addr-relay finding ("no queue, no poisson timer") is the visible half; whether the resulting cadence leaks topology is not knowable statically.

**8. SBCL-specific numeric and type behaviour.** Bignum promotion where Core wraps; `(signed-byte 32)` vs `(unsigned-byte 32)`; whether a declared type check *signals* or is *elided* at the current safety setting. GA10's #1 unverified S1 is precisely this — and its finder wrote that he could not confirm the runtime symptom because Docker was down. Also in this family: `%script-num` missing the CScriptNum sign byte; `CastToBool` on multi-byte negative zero; `(null #())` being false; SBCL eliding `coerce`+`reverse`. *Tool:* one `dev.sh eval` per claim. Cheapest verification available and this round did zero of it.

**9. Crash consistency and environment.** fsync ordering, partial writes, disk-full, file permissions, the flush/prune/index-write interleaving. `src/kv/fsync.lisp` and `src/kv/datadir.lisp` were not read; `src/node/indexes.lisp`'s own header describes an abandoned-chain window after a process kill and nobody checked it. *Tool:* a `kill -9`-at-each-phase restart matrix.

**And the oracle we already own and did not use.** `scripts/conformance.sh`'s own header says Core's functional suite is "the class of defect a 33k-check unit suite structurally cannot see." Baseline: **38 PASS / 185 FAIL / 23 SKIP / 17 TIMEOUT of 240**. GA10 ran **not one** of them. Several GA10 findings cite Core functional tests as *evidence by reading* (`rpc_users.py:178-181`, `feature_config_args.py:395`) without ever running them — those are one command from CONFIRMED or REFUTED.
